messages.author: 40cb5026d0e9f97c
messages.subject: marginal likelihood for logistic regression
parts:
Hi, 
I try to do model selection under various logistic regression models by computing the marginal likelihood.
In the two  examples below, log mlik is 0. 
Why is it so? 
What would be the most reliable strategy for model selection in logistic regression?
Thanks.
G.

require(INLA)
nsites <- 200
Ntrials <- rep(20,nsites)
b <- rnorm(n=1)
f <- 1/( 1 + exp(-(b)))
z <- rbinom(n=nsites,size=Ntrials,prob=f)
                    

res <- inla(formula=z~1,
            family="binomial",
            Ntrials=Ntrials,
            data = data.frame(z=z),
            control.data = list(link="logit",
              hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",param=c(0.1,0.1)))),
            control.fixed= list(prec.intercept = 1),
            control.compute = list(hyperpar=FALSE,return.marginals=FALSE,mlik=TRUE),
            control.inla=list(strategy = "laplace", npoints = 100))
res$mlik



y <- rnorm(nsites)
res <- inla(formula=z~1+y,
            family="binomial",
            Ntrials=Ntrials,
            data = data.frame(y=y,z=z),
            control.data = list(link="logit",
                 hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",param=c(0.1,0.1)))),
            control.fixed= list(prec.intercept = 1),
            control.compute = list(hyperpar=FALSE,return.marginals=FALSE,mlik=TRUE),
            control.inla=list(strategy = "laplace", npoints = 100))
res$mlik

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] marginal likelihood for logistic regression
parts:
The marginal likelihood is defined as the normalisation constant for the
hyperparameters; see the INLA paper. In your exmaples there is no
hyperparameters, so another estimate is needed in that case.
Unfortunately, it is not yet implemented in that case, therefore it
returns 0.

messages.author: 6b41239f795f4a4c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] marginal likelihood for logistic regression
parts:
Hi,
Could the CPO values help for model selection?
like
############

require(INLA)
nsites <- 200
Ntrials <- rep(20,nsites)
b <- rnorm(n=1)
f <- 1/( 1 + exp(-(b)))
z <- rbinom(n=nsites,size=Ntrials,prob=f)
res1 <- inla(formula=z~1,

family="binomial",
Ntrials=Ntrials,
data = data.frame(z=z),
control.data = list(link="logit",
hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",param=c(0.1,0.1)))),
control.fixed= list(prec.intercept = 1),
control.compute = list(cpo=T,hyperpar=FALSE,return.marginals=FALSE,mlik=TRUE),
control.inla=list(strategy = "laplace", npoints = 100))

res1$mlik

y <- rnorm(nsites)
res2 <- inla(formula=z~1+y,

family="binomial",
Ntrials=Ntrials,
data = data.frame(y=y,z=z),
control.data = list(link="logit",
hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",param=c(0.1,0.1)))),
control.fixed= list(prec.intercept = 1),
control.compute = list(cpo=T,hyperpar=FALSE,return.marginals=FALSE,mlik=TRUE),
control.inla=list(strategy = "laplace", npoints = 100))

res2$mlik

exp( sum(log(res1$cpo$cpo)) - sum(log(res2$cpo$cpo)) )

#######

Note I modified you example to have results in object of diff name and to calculate the CPO values.
> exp( sum(log(res1$cpo$cpo)) - sum(log(res2$cpo$cpo)) )
[1] 2.652227

What I am not sure here is whether one could interpret this value as an approximation to the Bayes factor. I imagine other reader could clarify that.
I think one of the ref in the paper section also deals with similar things but I am not an expert on this, so someone else's advice will be certainly more interesting.

best

Inti

messages.author: d531d68376255a20
messages.subject: Re: marginal likelihood for logistic regression
parts:
For what it's worth, using pure marginal likelihood for this task is
fairly dangerous. Marginal likelihood is very sensitive to the choice
of priors placed on parameters which only exist under some models,
both "interesting" parameters and nuisance ones. This is in stark
contrast to estimation, which can be very robust to choice of priors.
